title: The Ayniyya of Ibn Zurayq
intro: Ibn Zurayq al-Baghdadi addresses a woman who reproaches him for his endless travels, and remembers the one he loves, left behind in Karkh, a quarter of Baghdad, when he went away to seek his fortune. The poem moves from his plea against her blame to a portrait of a man driven from journey to journey, to thoughts on livelihood as God's to apportion, then to the farewell, his self-reproach, his sleepless nights and the deserted house, and it ends in patience and the hope of meeting again, or of following each other in death. Al-Sarraj, in Masari' al-Ushshaq, tells of a man from Baghdad who travelled to Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Andalusi and was given a meagre gift to test him; his spirit broke, and he fell ill and died in the inn where he lodged, with a sheet bearing lines of this poem at his head, and Abu Abd al-Rahman wept and sent five thousand dinars to his household in Baghdad. Al-Humaydi quotes Ibn Hazm: “It is said that whoever wears a carnelian ring, reads the Quran as Abu Amr read it, studies law in the school of al-Shafi'i and knows the poem of Ibn Zurayq by heart has perfected his refinement.”

translation: Do not blame him: blame only feeds his passion.
What you said is true, but he does not listen.
1.sharh: He begs a woman who reproaches him for leaving to stop: blame only makes him cling the more to what she blames. She is right, but he will not listen. Until line 15 he speaks of himself as “he”, as if pleading for someone else.

translation: You went so far in reproaching him that you harmed him,
where you thought reproach would do him good.
2.sharh: Her reproach has gone so far that it harms him, though she meant it to help. Advice pressed past its measure turns into injury and spoils what it set out to mend.

translation: Use gentleness, then, when you rebuke him,
not blame: his heart is wasted and in pain.
3.sharh: If she must rebuke him, let her do it gently and not with blame, for his heart is already worn out and aching, and it can bear no harshness.

translation: He was strong enough to shoulder any burden,
but the blows of fortune have pressed in his ribs.
4.sharh: Once he could shoulder any burden, but the blows of fortune have pressed in his ribs. The Arabic for “shouldering” comes from the word for a rib, so the frame that bore the weight is the one that gives way.

translation: Pain enough of scattering for him that every day
parting brings him something new to dread.
5.sharh: Every day parting brings him something new to dread, and that alone is pain enough of being torn from his people. Most sources read “the pain of reproach”: what parting does to him is punishment enough without her blame.

translation: He never comes home from a journey but a plan
for another journey stirs him, and he resolves on it.
6.sharh: No sooner is he home from one journey than a new plan unsettles him and sends him off on another, resolved before he has rested.

translation: It is as if, forever halting and setting off,
he were charged with pacing out God's wide earth.
7.sharh: Forever halting and setting off again, he is like a man appointed to pace out God's wide earth, as if measuring it step by step were his task.

translation: If fortune shows him wealth in travelling,
he is set on going, even if it be to Sind.
8.sharh: Let fortune show him wealth in some journey and he is set on going, even as far as Sind, the far end of the world for a man of Baghdad. Most of the older sources read “resolve” for “fortune”.

translation: His ambitions will have nothing but to load him
with toil for a living, and how many bid him farewell.
9.sharh: His ambitions will not let him rest; they load him with toil for a living, and he is forever being seen off by those he leaves behind.

translation: A man's struggling does not bring him a living,
nor does a man's ease cut him off from it.
10.sharh: Struggle does not bring a man his living, nor does ease cut him off from it: what is allotted to him will reach him whatever he does.

translation: God has shared out among His creatures their livings;
God created no creature to abandon it.
11.sharh: God has shared out their livelihoods among all He created, and made no creature only to abandon it. The thought echoes the Quran: “There is no creature on earth but its provision rests with God” (11:6).

translation: But they are saddled with greed: you will not see
one seeking a living content with less than the utmost.
12.sharh: Yet people are saddled with greed: you will not find one man seeking his living who is content with anything less than the utmost.

translation: Greed for a living, when livings are apportioned,
is aggression, and aggression brings a man down.
13.sharh: Greed for a living, when livings are already apportioned, is aggression, a reaching for what is not one's own, and aggression always brings down the man who commits it.

translation: Fortune gives a man, from where it seems to deny him,
an inheritance, and denies him where it raises his hopes.
14.sharh: Fortune is perverse: it brings a man an inheritance, wealth that comes through a death in his family, from the very quarter that seemed to deny him, and it withholds where it has raised his hopes. Neither effort nor expectation decides what he gets.

translation: I leave in God's keeping a moon of mine in Baghdad,
in Karkh, rising from the sphere of a buttoned collar.
15.sharh: He leaves in God's keeping the one he loves in Karkh, in Baghdad: a moon whose face rises from a buttoned collar as the moon rises in its sphere. Here the poet turns to “I”. It is among the poem's most quoted lines: Abu Hayyan al-Tawhidi cites it with the next, and Ibn Khallikan on its own.

translation: I bade him farewell, wishing that the sweetness of life
would bid me farewell, and I need not bid farewell to him.
16.sharh: He said goodbye wishing that it were the sweetness of life that left him, so that he need never say goodbye to his beloved. The words for farewell (wadda'a) and wish (wudd) chime through the line.

translation: How often he pleaded with me not to leave him,
but necessity has a state that grants no plea.
17.sharh: His beloved pleaded with him again and again not to go, but necessity has its own law, and it grants no plea. The verb for pleading and the verb for granting a plea come from the same root, so the plea meets its own refusal.

translation: How he clung to me on the morning I left,
my tears pouring down, and his tears too.
18.sharh: On the morning he left, his beloved clung to him, and both of them were in tears. The weeping is shared, as the sleeplessness and the faithfulness will be.

translation: I will not lie before God: the robe of my patience
is torn off me by parting from him, though I patch it.
19.sharh: He swears he will not lie before God: since the parting his patience hangs off him like a torn robe, and all he can do is patch it. Most sources read “the robe of my excuse”, which leads into the next line.

translation: I make my excuse wide for the wrong I did him
by leaving him, but my guilt will not let it be wide.
20.sharh: He looks for every excuse for the wrong he did his beloved by leaving, but his guilt is too large for any excuse to cover.

translation: I was given a kingdom and did not rule it well,
and whoever does not rule a kingdom well loses it.
21.sharh: Being near his beloved was a kingdom he was given and failed to rule, and whoever cannot govern a kingdom loses it. The line reads as a maxim, and Ibn Aydamir's anthology of choice lines picks it out from the poem and quotes it first.

translation: Whoever goes clothed in the robe of comfort
and gives no thanks for it, God will strip it from him.
22.sharh: Whoever is clothed in good fortune and gives no thanks for it, God strips it from him: the parting is the price of ingratitude. It echoes the Quran: “If you are grateful I will give you more” (14:7).

translation: In place of my friend's face, since we parted, I have
a cup from which he is made to drink what I am made to drink.
23.sharh: In place of his friend's face he has been given a bitter cup, and his friend is made to drink from it what he himself is made to drink: the two share the pain. Most sources read “from which he drank”, to the same effect; al-Kashkul reads “from which I am made to drink what I am made to drink”.

translation: Many a man tells me, “You have tasted parting”; I answer,
“The fault, by God, is mine; I do not deny it.”
24.sharh: Many say to him, “So you have tasted parting.” He answers that the fault, by God, is his own, and he does not deny it. Some sources read “It is parting's fault”, which sharpens his reply.

translation: If only I had stayed: all good sense lay in staying,
had I followed good sense the day it was clear.
25.sharh: If only he had stayed: all good sense lay in staying, had he followed it on the day it showed itself to him. He knew what was right and left it.

translation: I pass my days and use them up
in a grief for him that cuts my heart to pieces,
26.sharh: He spends his days and uses them up in grief for his beloved, a grief that cuts his heart to pieces: he cuts through his days while the grief cuts him.

translation: for one for whom, when sleepers sleep, I lie awake
burning with longing; my nights I do not sleep.
27.sharh: The grief is for one for whose sake, when everyone else is asleep, he lies awake in burning longing, never sleeping the night through.

translation: No bed lets my side rest, and likewise
his bed has given him no rest since I left.
28.sharh: No bed lets his side rest, and his beloved has found no rest in bed since he left: the sleeplessness is shared, and the second half repeats the first with the roles reversed.

translation: I never thought that fortune would bereave me
of him, nor that the days would bereave him of me,
29.sharh: He never thought that fortune would bereave him of his beloved, nor that the days would bereave his beloved of him. The loss runs both ways, as the sleeplessness did in the line before, and the sentence runs on into the next line.

translation: until parting came between us with a hand,
a left one, that denies me my share and denies him his.
30.sharh: Until parting came between them with an unlucky left hand, keeping from each his share of the other. The Arabs took the left as ill-omened, and bayn, “parting”, is also the word for “between”.

translation: I always dreaded and feared the turns of my fortune,
yet I was not spared the thing I dreaded.
31.sharh: He always dreaded the turns of fortune and trembled at them, yet he was not spared what he feared: dread does not avert fate.

translation: By God, house of our good life, whose traces
are worn away, whose grounds are effaced since I left:
32.sharh: He calls on the house where they lived their good life, its traces now worn away and its grounds effaced since he left. The old lament over a deserted campsite becomes a lament for a home.

translation: will time bring back our pleasure in you,
or will the nights that carried it off return it?
33.sharh: He asks the house whether time will bring back their pleasure in it, or the nights that carried it off will return it: the question of a man who knows the answer.

translation: In God's keeping be the one whose home you have become,
and may rain pour on your grounds and turn them green.
34.sharh: He commends to God's keeping his beloved, who still lives in the house, and prays that heavy rain will fall on it and turn its grounds green, an old Arab blessing on a beloved's home.

translation: The one who keeps a pledge to me he will not break,
as I keep a true pledge to him I will not break,
35.sharh: His beloved keeps a pledge to him that will not be broken, as he keeps a true pledge to his beloved: their faithfulness, like their tears and their sleeplessness, is mutual.

translation: the one whose memory splits my heart, and when
the memory of me crosses his heart, it splits it:
36.sharh: His beloved is the one whose memory splits his heart, and when the memory of him crosses his beloved's heart, it splits that heart too. The same verb closes both clauses: one grief in two hearts.

translation: I will be patient with a fortune that will not let me
enjoy him, nor let him enjoy me, in any state,
37.sharh: He swears to bear patiently a fortune that will not let him enjoy his beloved, nor let his beloved enjoy him, in any state at all. The oath is a vow of endurance, and the next line gives his reason.

translation: knowing that my endurance will bring relief after it,
and the tightest of straits, if you think on it, is the widest.
38.sharh: He holds to patience because he knows endurance brings relief, and that the tightest straits, looked at closely, are the widest. It recalls the Quran: “With hardship comes ease” (94:5).

translation: Perhaps the nights that wasted my body by our parting
will one day bring me together with him.
39.sharh: Perhaps the nights that wasted his body by keeping them apart will one day bring the two of them together again: he looks for reunion to the very nights that parted them. “Perhaps” is only a hope, and the last two lines face death and a parting without end.

translation: And if death carries off one of us,
the other will surely follow him the next day.
40.sharh: If death takes one of them, the other is bound to follow the next day, for neither can live without the other. The older sources have a single line in place of this one and the next.

translation: And if this parting lasts for ever for us,
what can we do against God's decree?
41.sharh: If this parting lasts for ever, there is nothing they can do against what God has decreed: the poem ends in surrender after hope.

1.1.5.head: أَولَعَ
1.1.5.meaning: Makes him the more attached; eggs him on.

4.1.3.head: مُضطَلِع
4.1.3.meaning: Strong enough to bear a load; the word comes from dil', a rib.

4.2.1.head: ضَيَّقَ
4.2.1.meaning: Were pressed in, made narrow. Most sources read fa-dulli'at, “were crushed”, and bayn, “parting”, for dahr, “fortune”.

5.1.4.head: التَّشتيت
5.1.4.meaning: Tashtit: scattering, being cast far from home.

6.2.5.head: أَزمَعَ
6.2.5.meaning: Resolves on it. Most sources read yujmi'uhu, with the same sense.

7.2.4.head: ذَرَعَ
7.2.4.meaning: Measures it by the forearm: crosses it as if pacing it out.

8.2.3.head: السِّند
8.2.3.meaning: Sind: the lands of the lower Indus, in today's Pakistan; for Baghdad, the far east.

9.1.5.head: جَشَّمَ
9.1.5.meaning: Burden him with something hard, against his will.

13.2.1.head: بَغي
13.2.1.meaning: Baghy: aggression, overstepping one's bounds to take what is not one's own.

14.2.1.head: إِرث
14.2.1.meaning: An inheritance. Al-Safadi, al-Suyuti and Ibn Aydamir read irban, “a wish, a need”.

15.1.1.head: اِستَودَعَ
15.1.1.meaning: “I leave in God's keeping”: the words of farewell, entrusting someone to God.

15.2.1.head: الكَرخ
15.2.1.meaning: Karkh: a large quarter of Baghdad on the west bank of the Tigris.

15.2.3-4.meaning: “The sphere of the buttons”: the collar, buttoned round the neck; falak is the circling path of a star or the moon.

16.1.2.head: وُدّ
16.1.2.meaning: Wudd: love, wish; bi-wuddi, “I would love it if”.

17.2.4.head: شَفَّعَ
17.2.4.meaning: Grants his plea, accepts his intercession.

19.1.1-3.meaning: “I will not lie before God”: an oath; I speak nothing but the truth.

19.1.4-5.meaning: “The robe of patience”: patience worn like a garment.

21.1.2.head: مُلك
21.1.2.meaning: Kingship, a kingdom: here the love he had and lost.

22.1.4-5.meaning: “The robe of comfort”: wealth and ease, worn like a garment.

23.1.4.head: خِلّ
23.1.4.meaning: Khill: a close, true friend; here the beloved.

24.1.4-5.meaning: “You have tasted parting”: now you know its bitterness.

25.1.1.meaning: Alla: “why did I not”, a particle of reproach with a past verb.

30.2.1.head: عَسراء
30.2.1.meaning: Asra': left, of a hand; the word also carries usr, hardship.

31.1.4.head: رَيب
31.1.4.meaning: Rayb: the turns and blows of fortune.

32.2.5.head: أَربُع
32.2.5.meaning: Arbu': plural of rab', a house and its grounds.

34.2.4.head: مَغنى
34.2.4.meaning: Maghna: an abode, where people live.

40.1.2.head: غالَ
40.1.2.meaning: Carries off, destroys unawares, as death does.
